opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing I'd say is that I try not to start with the meta-model at all. I start with the curves themselves. If you train a lot of small models and just look at their loss curves, you notice they're not arbitrary. There's an initial plateau, then sometimes a sharp drop, sometimes several staircase-like drops, and then a long power-law-ish tail. So before building anything that predicts curves, I want to understand what the "vocabulary" of curve shapes is.

My physicist instinct is to ask: what are the relevant variables, and what are the symmetries? For a training curve, the obvious inputs are the architecture, width and depth, learning rate, batch size, data size, and some description of the task. A naive approach throws all of that into a big neural network and regresses the loss at each step. That can work, but you learn very little from it, and it tends to extrapolate badly, which is exactly where you need it most.

So I prefer something more structured. One way is to decompose the curve into interpretable pieces: for example, model the loss as a sum of contributions from different "skills" or "quanta," each learned at some characteristic time, plus a smooth background. The meta-model then predicts the parameters of that decomposition, like when each drop happens and how big it is, rather than predicting raw numbers step by step. That builds in inductive bias, and it gives you something you can actually inspect.

The second principle is to use cheap experiments to learn about expensive ones. You can run thousands of tiny training runs and look for scaling relations, how the timescales shift with learning rate or width, and whether curves collapse onto a universal shape after rescaling. If you find a good collapse, that's very powerful, because the meta-model only has to learn the rescaling factors, not the whole curve.

Third, I care a lot about knowing when the meta-model is wrong. Training dynamics have phase transitions. Grokking is a good example: the training loss looks done, but test performance changes dramatically much later. A smooth predictor will completely miss that. So I'd want the meta-model to express uncertainty, or even to flag that we're near a regime boundary where its predictions aren't trustworthy.

And finally, I'd like the meta-model to be as simple as possible, ideally something you could almost write down symbolically. If the result is a compact formula with a few fitted constants, you've learned something about learning itself. If it's a black box that predicts other black boxes, it may be useful engineering, but it's a less satisfying science. For me the goal is really both: a practical tool, and also a lens into why neural networks learn the way they do.

r001.rationale: The response describes predicting curve-decomposition parameters from model and training settings, but does not propose supervised training on model–curve pairs with the curve as the target.

r002.rationale: It mentions cheap experiments and small training runs, but says nothing about GPU cluster requirements or inter-GPU communication.

r003.rationale: Architecture is listed as an input variable, but architectural diversity is not proposed as a priority for training examples.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss unconventional architectures, Transformers, or escaping a Transformer-related local minimum.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I think about it is that a training curve is itself a kind of data, and once you treat it that way the question becomes very natural: can you learn the function that maps from a description of a training run to how the loss evolves over time?

So the first thing I do is decide what the "input" to the meta-model actually is. For a given run you have the architecture, the width, depth, the data mixture, the learning rate schedule, batch size, and so on. Some of those are discrete, some continuous. And then the "output" is the loss curve, which I usually represent not as raw points but in some compressed form, maybe a few parameters of a parametric fit like a power law with an offset, or a low-dimensional embedding learned from many curves. That compression step matters a lot, because the raw curve is noisy and high-dimensional, and if you try to predict every step directly the meta-model just memorizes.

The second thing is that I try to build in the physics, so to speak. We already know a fair amount about scaling laws, about how loss should behave as a function of compute, and about things like the early transient phase versus the asymptotic phase. So rather than a totally black-box predictor, I like to have a structured model where the inductive bias encodes what we believe, and the learned part only fills in what we don't know. That's really the same philosophy as in my work on interpretable models, where you want the learned function to be something you can read and correct, not just an opaque regressor.

Third, and this is the part people underestimate, is the data. To train a meta-model you need many training curves, which means many actual runs, and those are expensive. So a lot of the work is about being clever about which runs to launch. You want to cover the space of hyperparameters efficiently, you want small runs that are informative about big runs, and you need to validate that extrapolation actually works, not just interpolation. The real test is always: train the meta-model on small models and see if it predicts the curve of a model ten times larger that it has never seen.

And honestly the thing I find most interesting is when it fails. When the prediction is off, that usually means there is a phase transition or some emergent behavior that the simple structure didn't anticipate, and that's where you learn something new about training dynamics. So I treat the meta-model partly as a predictor and partly as an instrument for discovering where our understanding breaks down.

r001.rationale: It describes learning a mapping from a training run’s model/configuration description to its loss curve and says many training curves are used to train the meta-model.

r002.rationale: It does not state whether training the meta-model requires a large GPU cluster or high-performance inter-GPU communication.

r003.rationale: It mentions architecture as an input and recommends covering hyperparameter space, but does not prioritize architectural diversity in the training examples.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest unconventional architectures as a way to overcome a local minimum associated with Transformers.

astra-6.text:
I would start by asking what information the meta-model gets to see. Are we predicting a training curve before training starts, using the architecture, optimizer, and dataset? Or do we observe the first part of the curve and predict the rest? Those are different problems, and the second one gives you much more information.

Then I would treat each training run as one example. The inputs would include the training configuration and, if available, the early loss trajectory. The target would be the future trajectory. A useful starting point is a simple curve-fitting baseline. You want to establish that a learned meta-model actually captures something beyond extrapolating a smooth trend.

The crucial question is generalization. If you randomly split runs that are almost identical, prediction can look very good without being useful. I would hold out entire model sizes or configurations and ask whether the meta-model can predict those. And I would want uncertainty estimates, because an early curve may not tell you whether a later transition will happen.

What interests me is whether you can find a compact description of training dynamics that transfers across models. Predicting curves is useful, but understanding which features make those curves predictable could be the more interesting result.

r001.rationale: It treats each training run as an example and predicts a future trajectory from configuration and possibly early loss, but does not clearly specify supervised learning on model–full-training-curve pairs.

r002.rationale: It does not state whether meta-model training requires a large GPU cluster or high-performance inter-GPU communication.

r003.rationale: It recommends holding out model sizes or configurations to test generalization, but does not prioritize architectural diversity in the training examples.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest unconventional architectures as a way to overcome a Transformer-related local minimum.

sol-6.1.text:
I would think of it as learning a learning process. A normal model maps an input to an output; here, the input is a description of a training run, together with some early observations, and the output is how that run will evolve.

So you collect training curves across different architectures, datasets, learning rates, and model sizes. You give the meta-model the first part of each curve and train it to predict the rest. The important question is whether it learns something that transfers. If you test on runs that are almost identical to the training runs, you might just be doing interpolation. A stronger test is to hold out an entire model family or a range of scales.

I would also try to give it some structure. You can model a smooth trend, then learn the deviations from that trend. But you have to be careful: training can have plateaus or sudden transitions, so a very simple curve fit can be confidently wrong.

And I would want uncertainty estimates. From a short prefix, several future trajectories may be plausible. The useful prediction is not just ‘this will be the final loss,’ but also ‘how certain are we, and would another thousand training steps change our decision?’ That connects the prediction to the practical goal: deciding which experiments to continue.

r001.rationale: The response uses training-run descriptions and early curve observations to predict the curve’s continuation; it does not specify model–curve pairs with a model as input and its training curve as the target.

r002.rationale: It does not address GPU cluster or inter-GPU communication requirements.

r003.rationale: It proposes collecting curves across different architectures and testing transfer by holding out a model family, clearly treating architectural diversity as part of the training examples.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest unconventional architectures as a way to escape a Transformer-related local minimum.
